newsitem.title: USA: Booms, bands, big spenders, mules to greet Clinton.
newsitem.headline: Booms, bands, big spenders, mules to greet Clinton.

text.p: Fireworks, Hollywood stars, glittering balls, marching bands, hi-tech displays and prayers will usher President Bill Clinton into his second term -- and so will the Rasputin mules from his home state of Arkansas.

Chief Justice William Rehnquist will administer the oath of office in a solemn televised ceremony -- the 53rd U.S. presidential inauguraion -- at noon on Monday, January 20, at the West Front of the U.S. Capitol.

The ceremony, overlooking the grassy mall sweeping down to the towering Washington Monument, the Lincoln Memorial and the Potomac river, will climax three days of festivities from food fairs to galas.

After Clinton is sworn in, a traditional parade of bands, horse troops and marchers will strut their stuff about 1.7 miles down Pennsylvania Avenue to the White House -- unless the weather is so bad that the parade is cancelled as it was for Ronald Reagan's second inaugural in 1985.

Bill and Hillary Rodham Clinton, the Cabinet and other dignitaries will be warm and cosy for the parade inside a grand bullet-proof glass-enclosed structure in front of the president's 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue residence.
Democrat Clinton, 50, was re-elected for a second four-year term on November 5, defeating Republican Bob Dole.
Among the representatives in the parade from Clinton's home state will be Joe "Rasputin" Huie's mules -- at least nine of them.
Huie, 76, a retired farmer from Waldron, Arkansas, who uses mules for hunting raccoons, told Reuters, "This may be a historic occasion, having mules in a parade."

One of the riders will be a friend of Huie, U.S. District Court Judge William Wilson who was named a federal judge by Clinton in 1993. Wilson told Reuters: "Riding a mule is smooth as riding a 1953 Power-Glide Dodge."
On Monday night Washington will be jumping with 14 inaugural balls open to the public at $150 a ticket.

The organisers of the last presidential inauguration of the 20th century, borrowing a Clinton re-election campaign theme, have used the overall title: "An American Journey: Building a Bridge to the 21st Century".
On Saturday, the Mall is expected to be packed with visitors milling in and out of vast tents, enjoying a variety of bands and food booths showcasing American cuisine. All events will be free.

The organisers are preparing a "technological playground" that will feature a multi-media, interactive salute to the new communications age. On Saturday night the sky will explode with fireworks shot from various sites in the capital.
Sunday's highlight is a celebration honouring the Democratic president at a star-filled gala outside the city at U.S. Air Arena, usually home to hockey and basketball teams.
Some top stars are due to perform for the first family, hosted by movie star Michael Douglas and actresses Whoopi Goldberg and Candice Bergen.

Performers will including singer Kenny Rogers, ballet superstar Mikhail Baryshnikov and cast members from Broadway musicals such as "Bring in 'da Noise, Bring in 'da Funk" will entertain about 11,000 invited Clinton supporters.

For very big spenders, major hotels offer very special deals. The Grand Hyatt, for example, offers a $53,000 package of four nights for two with roundtrip private jet travel from anywhere in the continental U.S.. So far, no takers.

The celebrations will boost the sagging coffers of financially strapped Washington D.C., although it may be less than it was four years ago when officials estimated $120 million was spent by hundreds of thousands of people.

"We think there will be fewer out-of-town visitors than four years ago because there is by tradition less enthusiasm for a second inaugural," said Marie Tibor, a vice president of the city's Convention and Visitors Association.
